items.title: ScaleODM
items.text:
Kubernetes-native orchestration for OpenDroneMap workloads, with a NodeODM-compatible API and S3-native task I/O.

Warning

ScaleODM does not provide authentication or authorization. Run it only on trusted private/internal networks. Do not expose the API directly to the public internet.

items.title: Quick start (Helm OCI)
items.text:
1. Create namespace and required runtime secret:
kubectl create namespace scaleodm

kubectl create secret generic scaleodm-secrets \
  --namespace scaleodm \
  --from-literal=SCALEODM_DATABASE_URL="postgresql://user:pass@your-db:5432/scaleodm?sslmode=require" \
  --from-literal=AWS_S3_ENDPOINT="https://s3.amazonaws.com" \
  --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="YOUR_ACCESS_KEY" \
  --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="YOUR_SECRET_KEY" \
  --from-literal=AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="us-east-1"
  1. Install the chart:
helm upgrade --install scaleodm oci://ghcr.io/hotosm/charts/scaleodm \
  --namespace scaleodm \
  --create-namespace \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --set database.external.enabled=true \
  --set s3.external.enabled=true \
  --set secrets.runtime.name="scaleodm-secrets" \
  --set argo.enabled=true
  1. Verify API connectivity (adjust host/port for your service exposure):
curl http://localhost:31100/info

See the Helm chart reference for all configuration options.

items.title: API smoke test
items.text:
# 1) Node info
curl http://localhost:31100/info

# 2) Create task (images must already exist in S3)
curl -X POST http://localhost:31100/task/new \
  -F "name=my-project" \
  -F "readS3Path=s3://mybucket/images/" \
  -F "writeS3Path=s3://mybucket/images/output/" \
  -F 'options=[{"name":"fast-orthophoto","value":true}]'

# 3) Check task status
curl http://localhost:31100/task/{uuid}/info

The full endpoint list is in the API reference.

items.title: About ScaleODM
items.text:
ScaleODM runs OpenDroneMap (ODM) processing on Kubernetes.

It is built for clusters that expect ephemeral jobs, declarative orchestration, and object storage. The existing ODM tools are excellent, but they were not designed with this in mind. This page explains where they struggle at scale, and why we took a different approach.

items.title: The existing tools
items.text:
ODM already has two tools for running jobs at scale:

  • NodeODM runs a single ODM job behind a REST API.
  • ClusterODM spreads jobs across several NodeODM instances.

Both are robust and widely used, and ODM itself is mature and well proven. None of what follows is a criticism of the projects. The problem is only their deployment model, which does not fit Kubernetes well.

items.title: Why NodeODM struggles to scale on Kubernetes
items.text: There are four main issues.

items.title: 1. ClusterODM scales machines, not containers
items.text:
ClusterODM scales by adding and removing whole machines (VMs). This works well for a pool of virtual machines.

Kubernetes scales differently. It thinks in terms of Jobs, Deployments, and autoscalers such as the HPA, KEDA, or Karpenter. ClusterODM uses none of these, so you lose the native scaling that Kubernetes is good at.

items.title: 2. NodeODM is a long-running, stateful server
items.text:
A NodeODM container is a server that stays running and keeps each project on local disk.

Kubernetes prefers pods that are ephemeral and stateless. They start, do one job, then go away. A long-lived server that holds state on local disk fights this model. It makes scaling down, and moving work between nodes, awkward.

items.title: 3. The NodeODM queue is local, not distributed
items.text:
NodeODM queues jobs using local files on a single instance. There is no shared queue across the cluster.

Once you want to run many jobs across many nodes, a local file-based queue is not enough to coordinate them.

items.title: 4. Getting imagery in means an upload
items.text:
NodeODM expects you to upload imagery over HTTP, or to pass a zip_url for it to download.

In our case the imagery already lives in S3. Pushing it back through an upload API is extra I/O and extra friction for no benefit. S3 is only supported for output too, so the input path still has to run through the API.

items.title: The ScaleODM approach
items.text:
ScaleODM drops the NodeODM and ClusterODM control plane. Instead it runs each ODM task directly as an Argo Workflow on Kubernetes.

Every task is one isolated workflow with three steps:

  1. Download the imagery from S3.
  2. Process it with the standard ODM container.
  3. Upload the results back to S3.

This maps cleanly onto how Kubernetes already works:

  • Jobs are stateless, isolated, and can be restarted if they fail.
  • Scaling, scheduling, retries, and cleanup are all handled by Kubernetes and Argo. We do not maintain our own queue or scaling glue.
  • S3 is the single source of truth for both input and output.

Importantly, ScaleODM still exposes a NodeODM-compatible API. Existing tools keep working, including pyodm's task monitoring and download methods. So you get Kubernetes-native scaling without rewriting your clients.

The main trade-off is that ScaleODM depends fully on Kubernetes, and on Argo Workflows being installed in the cluster. For our use, that is a fair price for scaling that just works.

items.title: A note on history (v1 to v2)
items.text:
The first version of ScaleODM kept NodeODM and ClusterODM, and added a queueing layer on top (PostgreSQL with SKIP LOCKED) plus some scaling glue.

It proved the queueing idea worked, but two problems remained. NodeODM's long-lived, stateful model still did not suit ephemeral workers, and getting imagery in still meant uploads or archive URLs.

v2 is the current approach described above: Argo Workflows, S3 for input and output, and a NodeODM-compatible API on top.

items.title: Decision records
items.text: For the full technical reasoning and architecture decisions, see the decision records.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
ScaleODM is a single Go service. It takes NodeODM-style API requests and runs each task as an Argo Workflow on Kubernetes. Imagery is read from S3 and results are written back to S3.

flowchart LR
    C[Client<br/>e.g. DroneTM, pyodm] -->|NodeODM API| API[ScaleODM API]
    API --> DB[(Postgres<br/>job metadata)]
    API -->|submit workflow| Argo[Argo Workflows]
    R[Reconciler] -->|poll status| Argo
    R --> DB
    R -->|webhook| C
    Argo --> Pod[ODM job pods]
    Pod -->|read images / write outputs| S3[(S3)]

items.title: Lifecycle of a task
items.text:
1. Submit. The client calls POST /task/new with readS3Path, writeS3Path and ODM options. The API checks the input, counts the images in S3 and works out how much CPU, memory and disk the job needs.
  2. Run. The API submits an Argo Workflow and records the job in Postgres. The workflow has three steps:
  3. download: rclone copies the images from S3 into a workspace volume.
  4. process: the ODM container runs on the images.
  5. upload: rclone copies the outputs to writeS3Path.
  6. Track. The reconciler is the only writer of job status. Every 30 seconds it saves Argo's phase for each unfinished job, and fails jobs whose workflow has gone missing. GET /task/{uuid}/info and the UI only read: they show the live Argo phase until the job finishes, then the saved status. Pod errors such as an image pull failure show as failed while they last, but are not saved, because Argo can still recover.
  7. Notify. When a job finishes or fails, the reconciler calls the client's webhook, if one was given.

There is no queue of its own. Argo and the Kubernetes scheduler (with Karpenter on AWS) decide when and where pods run.

items.title: Code layout
items.text: Path Purpose main.go Startup: config, database, Argo client, reconciler, HTTP server. app/api/ NodeODM-compatible HTTP API (/task/*, /info, health checks). app/workflows/ Builds Argo Workflow specs and sizes resources by image count. app/workflows/scripts/ Shell scripts run by each workflow step. app/reconciler/ Background loop that syncs Argo status to the database and calls webhooks. app/meta/ Job metadata store (reads and writes to Postgres). app/db/ Database connection and schema.sql. app/s3/ S3 helpers: listing images, output files, download filters. app/config/ Environment variable config and defaults. app/ui/ Small web UI at /ui for browsing jobs (read-only by default). chart/ Helm chart for ScaleODM, with optional Argo and Postgres.

items.title: Further reading
items.text:
• About: why ScaleODM exists, compared with NodeODM and ClusterODM.
  • Memory sizing and swap: how job resources are calculated.
  • Decision records: Argo, S3 credentials and swap.

items.title: NodeODM API Compatibility
items.text:
ScaleODM implements the NodeODM API, but stores data in S3 and runs jobs as Argo Workflows. This makes it a drop-in, scalable replacement for NodeODM.

Just want the shortest pyodm migration path? Start with the quick migration guide, then come back here for the full endpoint and behaviour reference.

items.title: Quick Start: Deploy to Existing Cluster
items.text:
If you already have Argo Workflows installed in an argo namespace:

# 1. Create the namespace
kubectl create namespace scaleodm

# 2. Create the required runtime secret
kubectl create secret generic scaleodm-secrets \
  --namespace scaleodm \
  --from-literal=SCALEODM_DATABASE_URL="postgresql://user:pass@your-db:5432/scaleodm?sslmode=require" \
  --from-literal=AWS_S3_ENDPOINT="https://s3.amazonaws.com" \
  --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="YOUR_ACCESS_KEY" \
  --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="YOUR_SECRET_KEY" \
  --from-literal=AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="us-east-1"

# 3. Install the chart (skip Argo subchart since you already have it)
helm install scaleodm ./chart \
  --namespace scaleodm \
  --set argo.enabled=false \
  --set database.external.enabled=true \
  --set s3.external.enabled=true \
  --set secrets.runtime.name="scaleodm-secrets"

# 4. Verify
kubectl get pods -n scaleodm
curl http://scaleodm.scaleodm.svc.cluster.local:31100/info

The API is now available at scaleodm.scaleodm.svc.cluster.local:31100 from within the cluster.

items.title: How It Works
items.text:
The processing pipeline for each task:

  1. Task creation - POST /task/new with an S3 path (via zipurl or readS3Path)
  2. Download stage - Argo workflow pod uses rclone to copy images from S3 to local disk. Supports raw images (jpg/tif) and archives (zip/tar/tar.gz) which are auto-extracted and flattened.
  3. Process stage - ODM container processes the images
  4. Upload stage - rclone pushes results back to S3 (to writeS3Path or {zipurl}-output/)
  5. Query results - GET /task/{uuid}/info for status, GET /task/{uuid}/assets for output discovery, and GET /task/{uuid}/download/{asset} for the canonical 302 redirect flow to pre-signed S3 URLs

items.title: Using with pyodm
items.text:
pyodm's create_task() uses NodeODM's chunked upload flow (/task/new/init + /task/new/upload + /task/new/commit) which ScaleODM does not implement - ScaleODM processes images already in S3.

However, pyodm works with ScaleODM for task creation via Node.post() and for all monitoring/download operations via the standard Task class. No custom wrapper package needed.

items.title: Create tasks with pyodm + S3
items.text:
import json
from pyodm import Node
from pyodm.api import Task

node = Node("scaleodm.scaleodm.svc.cluster.local", 31100)

# Create task - use Node.post() to send zipurl directly
result = node.post("/task/new", data={
    "name": "my-project",
    "zipurl": "s3://mybucket/drone-images/",
    "options": json.dumps([
        {"name": "fast-orthophoto", "value": True},
        {"name": "dsm", "value": True},
    ]),
})
uuid = result.json()["uuid"]
print(f"Task created: {uuid}")

# Wrap in a pyodm Task for monitoring - all standard methods work
task = Task(node, uuid)

# Poll status
info = task.info()
print(f"Status: {info.status}")       # TaskStatus enum
print(f"Progress: {info.progress}%")

# Block until complete
task.wait_for_completion()

# Download results (follows redirect to pre-signed S3 URL)
task.download_assets("/tmp/results/")

items.title: Helper function for cleaner integration
items.text:
If you're replacing NodeODM in an existing app, add this helper:

import json
from pyodm import Node
from pyodm.api import Task


def create_s3_task(node, s3_path, name="odm-project", options=None):
    """Create a ScaleODM task from an S3 path of images.

    Args:
        node: pyodm Node pointed at ScaleODM
        s3_path: S3 path containing images (e.g. "s3://bucket/images/")
        name: Project name
        options: Dict of ODM options (e.g. {"dsm": True})

    Returns:
        pyodm Task object (supports .info(), .wait_for_completion(),
        .download_assets(), etc.)
    """
    odm_options = []
    if options:
        for k, v in options.items():
            odm_options.append({"name": k, "value": v})

    data = {
        "name": name,
        "zipurl": s3_path,
    }
    if odm_options:
        data["options"] = json.dumps(odm_options)

    result = node.post("/task/new", data=data)
    return Task(node, result.json()["uuid"])


# Usage - almost identical to pyodm's create_task():
node = Node("scaleodm-host", 31100)
task = create_s3_task(
    node,
    "s3://mybucket/drone-images/",
    name="my-project",
    options={"fast-orthophoto": True, "dsm": True},
)
task.wait_for_completion()
task.download_assets("/tmp/results/")

items.title: Migration from NodeODM
items.text:
Replace your existing create_task() calls:

# BEFORE (NodeODM - uploads files directly):
task = node.create_task(
    ["img1.jpg", "img2.jpg", ...],
    options={"dsm": True},
)

# AFTER (ScaleODM - images pre-uploaded to S3):
task = create_s3_task(
    node,
    "s3://mybucket/project/images/",
    options={"dsm": True},
)

# Everything else stays the same:
task.wait_for_completion()
task.download_assets("/tmp/results/")
info = task.info()
task.cancel()
task.remove()

items.title: GET /info
items.text:
Returns node information including queue count and engine version.

{
  "version": "<chart appVersion>",
  "taskQueueCount": 5,
  "maxImages": null,
  "engine": "odm",
  "engineVersion": "docker.io/opendronemap/odm:3.6.2"
}

items.title: GET /options
items.text: Returns available ODM processing options.

items.title: POST /task/new
items.text:
Creates a new processing task.

Parameters (form-encoded or JSON body):

Parameter Required Description zipurl * S3 path to images (e.g. s3://bucket/images/). NodeODM-compatible. readS3Path * S3 path to images. Preferred for new integrations. writeS3Path S3 path for outputs. Defaults to readS3Path/output/. name Task name. Defaults to odm-project. options JSON array: [{"name": "dsm", "value": true}] s3Endpoint Custom S3 endpoint (MinIO, Garage, etc.). Must be reachable from workflow pods. s3Region S3 region. Defaults to us-east-1. webhook Callback URL on completion. skipPostProcessing Skip point cloud tiles. processingMode Pipeline mode. See Processing Modes. Defaults to standard. s3ScanDepth Max depth for the rclone scan beneath readS3Path. Defaults to 1 (just the given dir). Range: 1-10. See Scan depth. excludePaths JSON array of rclone-style filter patterns appended to the default exclude set. useDefaultExcludes Apply the built-in ODM-output exclude list. Defaults to true.

* One of zipurl or readS3Path is required. Both must be s3:// paths.

When using zipurl, outputs are written to {zipurl}-output/. When using readS3Path, outputs default to readS3Path/output/ (or explicit writeS3Path).

items.title: Processing modes
items.text:
processingMode selects the pipeline shape. Today only standard is implemented; the reserved modes are recognised so clients can probe support and fail fast (HTTP 501).

Mode Status Behaviour standard implemented (default) The regular ODM pipeline: download → process → upload. Imagery under readS3Path is gathered into a single ODM run. How wide the input scan is is configured separately via s3ScanDepth - use depth 1 for one task's images dir, or a higher value to roll up several task subdirs under a project root. merge-existing reserved (501) Given a project root that already contains per-task ODM outputs, run only the merge half of split-merge to stitch the existing orthos, DEMs, and point clouds into a single set of products. The "split" half is assumed already complete, which is much cheaper than re-running per-task processing from raw imagery. thermal reserved (501) Dedicated pipeline for thermal imagery: applies a thermal-specific pre-processing stage (radiometric handling, alignment) before the ODM run. Implementation deferred. city-scale reserved (501) Large-area (>40 km²) projects requiring corrective alignment. The pipeline iteratively fans out from a central anchor task, aligning each subsequent task against prior LAZ point clouds, then runs a final alignment pass against a global DEM. Implementation deferred.

Reserved modes return HTTP 501 with a clear message so clients can probe support.

items.title: Scan depth
items.text:
s3ScanDepth caps how deep the download stage walks beneath readS3Path. It maps directly to rclone's --max-depth N.

s3ScanDepth Behaviour When to use 1 (default) Only files in the given directory itself. readS3Path already points at the imagery dir, e.g. s3://bucket/project-id/task-id/images/. 2-10 Walks N levels of subdirectories. readS3Path points at a higher-level prefix that contains nested task layouts. For DroneTM-style projectid/taskid/images/*.jpg, a depth of 3 against s3://bucket/projectid/ will pick up imagery in every task subdir in one run. 0/unset Resolved to the default (1). -

Values outside 1-10 are rejected with HTTP 400.

items.title: Exclude patterns
items.text:
The download stage applies a default exclude list when useDefaultExcludes is true (the default). The current default set is:

odm_orthophoto/**
odm_dem/**
odm_dem_tiles/**
odm_texturing/**
odm_texturing_25d/**
odm_meshing/**
odm_filterpoints/**
odm_georeferencing/**
odm_report/**
images_resize/**
entwine_pointcloud/**
mapproxy/**
submodels/**
*-output/**
all.zip
**/all.zip

These are rclone filter patterns: dir/** matches the directory at any depth and excludes its contents. The all.zip entries are critical - the download stage auto-extracts archives with junk-paths, so a stray all.zip from a prior run would otherwise dump every flattened orthophoto/DSM/log file into the input image dir.

Set useDefaultExcludes: false only if you genuinely want to re-process a prior run's output as input.

excludePaths accepts a JSON array of additional patterns, validated for path traversal (..), absolute paths (leading /), embedded newlines, and shell metacharacters. Patterns are written to a --filter-from file at workflow runtime, so they never touch a shell.

Example - roll up every task under a project root into one run, deeper scan, and ignore a custom scratch dir:

curl -X POST http://scaleodm:31100/task/new \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "project-123",
    "readS3Path": "s3://mybucket/project-123/",
    "processingMode": "standard",
    "s3ScanDepth": 3,
    "excludePaths": "[\"scratch/**\", \"*.bak\"]"
  }'

items.title: Workspace file options
items.text:
boundary and cameras accept inline JSON (string or object), an s3:// URL, or a plain ODM file path. Inline and S3 documents are written to the workspace before processing and preserved on restart when options is omitted.

S3 documents are validated on submission; missing, unreadable, empty or invalid files return 400. Inline limits are 256 KiB for boundaries and 64 KiB for cameras to keep workflow specs small. Use S3 for larger documents.

items.title: Boundary
items.text: --boundary clips the reconstruction to one Polygon, supplied as a geometry, Feature, or single-feature FeatureCollection. It requires a non-empty ring of numeric coordinate pairs and is saved as /workspace/{workflow}/boundary.geojson.

items.title: Cameras
items.text:
--cameras supplies camera intrinsics. The document must be a non-empty object keyed by ODM camera ID. Each entry requires projection_type, positive integer width and height, and both focal_x and focal_y if either is set.

IDs require at least six space-separated parts, such as dji fc8482 4032 3024 brown 0.6666; the v2 prefix is accepted. Shorter IDs return 400 because ODM silently discards them.

Calibration is saved as /workspace/{workflow}/cameras-input.json to avoid ODM overwriting it. ScaleODM does not add --use-fixed-camera-params.

If s3Endpoint is provided, ScaleODM applies that endpoint to workflow pods and API-side S3 operations (image counting, workspace file preflight, log fallback, and pre-signed downloads). When it is omitted, both fall back to the deployment's AWS_S3_ENDPOINT, so the API and the workflow always resolve against the same store. Endpoints are normalized to scheme+host[:port]; whether a store is treated as AWS or as S3-compatible is decided by host, so an explicit s3.amazonaws.com keeps AWS addressing rather than being forced to path-style.

Response: {"uuid": "odm-pipeline-abc123"}

items.title: GET /task/{uuid}/info
items.text:
Returns task status. The status field is a nested object matching NodeODM spec:

{
  "uuid": "odm-pipeline-abc123",
  "name": "my-project",
  "dateCreated": 1705334400,
  "processingTime": 120000,
  "status": { "code": 20 },
  "options": [{ "name": "fast-orthophoto", "value": true }],
  "imagesCount": 0,
  "progress": 50,
  "output": ["Processing images..."]
}

Failed tasks include an error message: {"status": {"code": 30, "errorMessage": "..."}}

Status codes: 10=QUEUED, 20=RUNNING, 30=FAILED, 40=COMPLETED, 50=CANCELED

items.title: GET /task/{uuid}/output
items.text: Console output. Query param line to start from a specific line.

items.title: GET /task/{uuid}/assets
items.text:
Additive convenience endpoint for explicit output discovery.

Query params:

  • includeAdditional (default false): when true, includes discovered non-primary files.
  • additionalLimit (default 100, max 1000): cap for additional discovered files.

Response shape:

{
  "primary": [
    {
      "id": "all_zip",
      "asset": "all.zip",
      "exists": true,
      "downloadUrl": "/task/odm-pipeline-abc/download/all.zip"
    },
    {
      "id": "point_cloud",
      "asset": "georeferenced_model.laz",
      "exists": false
    }
  ],
  "additional": [
    {
      "asset": "report.pdf",
      "downloadUrl": "/task/odm-pipeline-abc/download/report.pdf"
    }
  ]
}

Primary assets are always returned as exists/missing using a bounded check set (all.zip, orthophoto.tif, dsm.tif, dtm.tif, and first-match point-cloud candidates).

items.title: GET /task/{uuid}/download/{asset}
items.text: Canonical download endpoint. Returns HTTP 302 redirect to a pre-signed S3 URL (1 hour expiry). The new /assets endpoint returns URLs pointing here (not direct pre-signed URLs), so existing redirect semantics remain unchanged.

items.title: POST /task/cancel
items.text: Body: {"uuid": "..."} → {"success": true}

items.title: POST /task/remove
items.text: Body: {"uuid": "..."} → {"success": true}

items.title: POST /task/restart
items.text:
Body: {"uuid": "...", "options": "[...]"} → {"success": true}

Omitting options reuses the stored flags, files and odmImage.

items.title: Key Differences from NodeODM
items.text: NodeODM ScaleODM Image input Upload via multipart form S3 path via zipurl or readS3Path Chunked upload /task/new/init + /upload + /commit Not implemented (not needed) Downloads Direct binary response 302 redirect to pre-signed S3 URL UUIDs Random UUID Argo workflow name (odm-pipeline-xxxxx) Scaling Single machine Kubernetes + Argo Workflows Image formats Upload any file S3 dir with jpg/tif (or zip/tar archives)

items.title: Status Mapping
items.text:
Argo Phase NodeODM Code Status Pending 10 QUEUED Running 20 RUNNING Succeeded 40 COMPLETED Failed 30 FAILED Error 30 FAILED

A Running workflow whose pod hits an infrastructure error (image pull failure, missing secret) is reported as 30 with that error while it lasts. It is not saved, so the status returns to the live phase if Argo recovers. Clients that treat 30 as final, such as pyodm's wait_for_completion(), stop at that point.

items.title: Helm Values for External Argo + External DB + External S3
items.text:
# values-production.yaml
argo:
  enabled: false # Use your existing Argo Workflows installation

database:
  external:
    enabled: true

s3:
  external:
    enabled: true

secrets:
  runtime:
    name: "scaleodm-secrets"
    keys:
      databaseUrl: "SCALEODM_DATABASE_URL"
      s3Endpoint: "AWS_S3_ENDPOINT"
      accessKey: "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"
      secretKey: "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
      region: "AWS_DEFAULT_REGION"

api:
  replicaCount: 2 # HA - also creates a PodDisruptionBudget

config:
  odmImage: "docker.io/opendronemap/odm:3.6.2"

helm install scaleodm ./chart -n scaleodm -f values-production.yaml

items.title: S3 Structure
items.text:
Single-task layout (default - s3ScanDepth: 1):

s3://mybucket/
  └── project-123/
      ├── images/            ← zipurl/readS3Path points here
      │   ├── DJI_0001.jpg
      │   ├── DJI_0002.jpg
      │   └── ...
      └── images-output/     ← auto-created by ScaleODM (zipurl mode)
          ├── odm_orthophoto/
          │   └── odm_orthophoto.tif
          ├── odm_dem/
          │   ├── dsm.tif
          │   └── dtm.tif
          └── ...

Multi-task layout (set s3ScanDepth deep enough to reach the imagery - typically 3 for projectid/taskid/images/*.jpg) - point readS3Path at the project root and ScaleODM gathers every task's imagery into one run:

s3://mybucket/project-123/   ← readS3Path points here
  ├── task-a/
  │   ├── images/
  │   │   ├── DJI_0001.jpg
  │   │   └── DJI_0002.jpg
  │   └── output/            ← excluded by default
  │       └── odm_orthophoto/odm_orthophoto.tif
  ├── task-b/
  │   └── images/
  │       ├── DJI_0101.jpg
  │       └── DJI_0102.jpg
  └── output/                ← project-level output written here

items.title: Testing
items.text:
# Verify API is up
curl http://scaleodm:31100/info

# Create a task
curl -X POST http://scaleodm:31100/task/new \
  -F "zipurl=s3://mybucket/images/" \
  -F 'options=[{"name":"fast-orthophoto","value":true}]'

# Check status
curl http://scaleodm:31100/task/odm-pipeline-xxxxx/info

# Download (follows redirect)
curl -L http://scaleodm:31100/task/odm-pipeline-xxxxx/download/orthophoto.tif -o orthophoto.tif

items.title: Not Implemented
items.text:
• File uploads via /task/new/init, /task/new/upload, /task/new/commit (chunked upload)
  • HTTP zip URL downloads (only s3:// paths supported)
  • Auth endpoints (/auth/login, /auth/info)
  • imagesCount (always 0)

items.title: pyodm migration: NodeODM to ScaleODM (quick guide)
items.text: This guide covers the smallest code change needed to keep using pyodm with ScaleODM.

items.title: What changes, and what stays the same
items.text:
Only one thing changes: task creation. node.create_task([...]) uploads local files, but ScaleODM expects the images to already be in S3.

Everything else stays the same. Once you have a task UUID, the pyodm Task methods still work as before, for status polling, waiting, cancel/remove, and asset downloads.

items.title: Minimal create-task migration
items.text:
# BEFORE (NodeODM)
from pyodm import Node

node = Node("nodeodm-host", 3000)
task = node.create_task(["img1.jpg", "img2.jpg"])

# AFTER (ScaleODM)
import json
from pyodm import Node
from pyodm.api import Task

node = Node("scaleodm-host", 31100)

resp = node.post("/task/new", data={
    "name": "my-project",
    # Use either readS3Path or zipurl
    "readS3Path": "s3://mybucket/project/images/",
    # Optional but recommended for explicit output location
    "writeS3Path": "s3://mybucket/project/output/",
    # Optional: specify additional config options
    "options": json.dumps([
        {"name": "fast-orthophoto", "value": True}
    ]),
})

uuid = resp.json()["uuid"]
task = Task(node, uuid)

items.title: Simplest status workflow
items.text:
info = task.info()
print(info.status, info.progress)

task.wait_for_completion()

items.title: Simplest output workflow
items.text:
task.download_assets("/tmp/results/")

ScaleODM download endpoints use redirect-backed downloads (HTTP 302 to pre-signed S3 URLs). download_assets(...) handles this flow.

items.title: Gotchas
items.text:
• Input images must already exist in S3 before calling /task/new.
  • If you pass s3Endpoint per task (for MinIO/Garage/etc.), it must be reachable from workflow pods, not only from your client machine.

items.title: Need full endpoint/reference details?
items.text: See NodeODM API compatibility reference.

items.title: Swap-based memory sizing
items.text:
ScaleODM's image-count estimate is a brief peak, not the resident set. So it requests steady-state RAM only and lets the kernel spill the peak to swap under Kubernetes' LimitedSwap policy:

request (real RAM)     = peak / (1 + SWAP_RATIO)             # prod 1.0 -> ~half of peak
limit  (resident cap)  = request * (1 + MARGIN_PERCENT/100)  # swap on: < node RAM
limit  (OOM ceiling)   = peak    * (1 + MARGIN_PERCENT/100)  # swap off: whole peak as RAM

The limit is memory.max, which caps resident memory. With swap on it targets below node RAM so the kernel is forced to push the peak out. Land it above node RAM and the cgroup gets no pressure, resident fills the node, and kubelet's swap-blind node-pressure eviction kills the pod with swap still free. request < limit keeps the pod Burstable, which is what earns it a swap grant. Guaranteed pods (request == limit) get none.

Warning

"Below node RAM" isn't guaranteed. Karpenter picks the node after sizing, so a request just under a node's allocatable leaves no room for the margin (request 113Gi on a 128Gi node gives a 136Gi limit). Node reclaim tuning below is the backstop. Watch jobs whose request sits near a node-size boundary.

kubelet grants swap proportionally, not the full limit - request:

pod swap = request / node_RAM * node_swap

So the node needs enough swap that this grant covers the peak, or the peak still OOMs. Workflows carry scaleodm.hotosm.org/burst-headroom-gib (limit - request) as a rough guide; the real allowance is container_swap_limit_bytes.

Validated in production. A 12k-image job pushed 344 GiB through swap while pinned at memory.max for 27 minutes in OpenMVS densify, and completed. A later run of the same imagery with a real --boundary never touched swap: the peak fell below memory.max and node RAM absorbed it.

Rationale and headroom analysis: decision 0003.

items.title: Two layers
items.text:
• Node: swap exists and kubelet allows it. Platform-specific, below.
  • Workload: the pod sets request < limit (Burstable), so the kernel grants it swap. Platform-agnostic, so ScaleODM never needs to know how a node got its swap.

kubelet config is the same everywhere; only the node bootstrap differs:

failSwapOn: false
memorySwap:
  swapBehavior: LimitedSwap
# featureGates: { NodeSwap: true }   # only on older kubelets where NodeSwap is beta

items.title: AWS / Karpenter (default)
items.text:
ScaleODM runs on its own dedicated, tainted pool so swap nodes aren't shared. In k8s-infra:

  • apps/karpenter/scaleodm-nodepool.yaml: Intel *id (local-NVMe) pool, labelled pool=scaleodm, tainted dedicated=scaleodm:NoSchedule.
  • apps/karpenter/scaleodm-ec2nodeclass.yaml: userData puts a 2x-RAM swap file on the NVMe instance store (instanceStorePolicy: RAID0, ~100x faster than EBS), sets the kubelet flags above, and tunes the VM: vm.swappiness=10 to keep the hot set in RAM outside the peak, plus vm.min_free_kbytes and vm.watermark_scale_factor so kswapd reclaims early and a fast fusion spike can't outrun it into eviction.

ScaleODM targets the pool with nodeSelector=pool=scaleodm, tolerations=dedicated=scaleodm:NoSchedule, schedulingMode=karpenter.

Fail-closed: a kubelet drop-in makes kubelet Requires= the swap unit, so swap is on before kubelet reads capacity. If swap setup fails the node never goes Ready and Karpenter replaces it, rather than joining swapless and OOM-killing a multi-hour job.

items.title: Verify a node
items.text:
A Ready node already implies swap succeeded, via that gate. To confirm:

# host swap: expect ~2x RAM on /mnt/k8s-disks/0/swapfile
swapon --show

# pod swap allowance. Target the worker container, NOT the default:
# kubectl exec defaults to a 2Gi sidecar. Containers: wait / download / process / upload.
# Check this FIRST on an eviction or OOM. Must be roughly request/node_RAM * node_swap,
# not just > 0. Zero means no grant and it will OOM at the peak.
kubectl -n odm exec <pod> -c process -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.swap.max

On a new dataset, watch the densify/fuse and mvs-texturing peaks: memory.swap.current should climb, memory.events should show no OOM, node memory.available should stay above 100Mi. Worst case is a contained cgroup OOM, not a node-level eviction.

kubectl -n odm exec <pod> -c process -- grep -H . \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.peak \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.swap.current /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.swap.peak \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.swap.max /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.swap.events

items.title: Generic / self-managed (Hetzner, kubeadm, k3s, bare metal)
items.text:
Note

With a huge-RAM machine, skip swap entirely.

Switching schedulingMode isn't enough. Nodes must support swap and pods must be pinned to them, or a reduced request just OOMs. Needs cgroups v2, a swap-capable kubelet, and ideally a fast, encrypted, dedicated swap disk.

  1. Create and persist swap on each node:
sudo fallocate -l 128G /swapfile   # ~2x RAM
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

  1. Add the kubelet config above to /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (or a k3s kubelet-arg drop-in), restart kubelet, label the nodes (kubectl label node <n> pool=swap).

  2. Point ScaleODM at them. The selector is required, or pods OOM on non-swap nodes:

SCALEODM_WORKFLOW_SCHEDULING_MODE=generic
SCALEODM_WORKFLOW_NODE_SELECTOR=pool=swap
SCALEODM_WORKFLOW_TOLERATIONS=              # e.g. swap=true:NoSchedule if tainted

items.title: Options
items.text: Env / Helm value Default Purpose SCALEODM_PROCESS_SWAP_RATIO / processSizing.swapRatio 0 (prod 1.0) request = peak/(1+ratio); 0 disables. Only set > 0 with a swap-node selector SCALEODM_PROCESS_MEMORY_REQUEST_MIN_GIB / processSizing.memoryRequestMinGiB 4 floor for the RAM request SCALEODM_PROCESS_MEMORY_LIMIT_MARGIN_PERCENT 20 limit margin. Swap off: above the peak. Swap on: above the request SCALEODM_PROCESS_CPU_PER_GIB / processSizing.cpuPerGiB 0.125 CPU request per GiB of RAM request (0.125 = r-family) SCALEODM_PROCESS_CPU_LIMIT_MULTIPLIER / processSizing.cpuLimitMultiplier 1.5 (prod 0) CPU limit = request x this; 0 omits it so ODM bursts to every core SCALEODM_WORKFLOW_ONDEMAND_IMAGE_THRESHOLD / config.workflow.onDemandImageThreshold 5000 auto-upgrade spot to on-demand at/above this count; 0 disables SCALEODM_WORKFLOW_SCHEDULING_MODE / config.workflow.schedulingMode karpenter karpenter or generic SCALEODM_WORKFLOW_NODE_SELECTOR / config.workflow.nodeSelector node-type=cpu base node selector SCALEODM_WORKFLOW_TOLERATIONS / config.workflow.tolerations "" extra tolerations

items.title: Memory sizing
items.text: How much RAM (and swap) an ODM run needs, by image count. For how ScaleODM turns these into pod requests and limits see swap sizing and decision 0003.

items.title: The short version
items.text:
• RAM demand is a brief peak, not sustained.
  • The table is RAM + swap. Provision less real RAM and let swap cover the peak. With ~2x swap a 62Gi machine handles ~5000 images.
  • Past ~5000 images the peak lands in OpenMVS DensifyPointCloud and grows faster than linearly. It scales with view count, not depth-map resolution.
  • Always pass a real --boundary. Render cost tracks reconstruction extent, so bad geometry is a sizing problem too.
Images RAM + swap 40 4 GB 250 16 GB 500 32 GB 1500 64 GB 2500 128 GB 3500 192 GB 5000 256 GB 12000 800 GB

Don't go much past 12000 in one scene. Above that use --split / --split-overlap and let ODM build and merge submodels. Still one pod, no fan out.

items.title: Prod sizing at 12k
items.text:
memoryMaxGiB 1200, swapRatio 1.0, memoryLimitMarginPercent 20, cpuPerGiB 0.125, ephemeralGiBPerGiBRAM 0.3:

peak est request memory.max CPU ephemeral node 12k 800 400 GiB 480 GiB 50 240 GiB r6id.16xlarge
  • Sizing counts S3 objects, ODM counts usable images. One 12k run sized off

    = 12000 while ODM loaded 11782.

items.title: Observed
items.text:
64 GB RAM (12 core), no swap: ~4000 image ceiling. With ~2x swap (127 GB):

  • Comfortable to ~1600, swap nearly gone at 1869.
  • 2658 images: out of swap, OOM-killed in OpenMVS, recovers and finishes.
  • 4778 images: OOM-killed in OpenMVS, again in mvs-texturing, dies.
  • ~144 GB peak at 3000 images, so ~4000 per submodel is the practical limit. Freetown WJ (34k images) used --split 8000.

~12k images, ODX 3.8.3, --sfm-algorithm triangulation. Same imagery both columns, the difference is --boundary plus dropping --matcher-neighbors and --use-hybrid-bundle-adjustment:

Unbounded, 384 GiB node --boundary, 768 GiB node memory.max 360 GiB 720 GiB Working-set peak 932 GiB (medium, killed) / 709 GiB (low) 649 GiB DensifyPointCloud VmPeak 709 GiB 89.8 GiB Swap used 344 GiB, 27 min pinned 0 B odm_dem + odm_orthophoto pinned memory.max 1h52m, 419 GiB swap no pressure Ortho / DEM raster 77 / 46.8 Gpixels, 92% cropped 8.24 / 4.18 Gpixels, 0% cropped Wall clock 17h57m 11h47m
  • Quartering depth-map pixels moved the peak only ~25%, so pc-quality is the wrong flag to optimise. Size the node instead.
  • Fusion 67 GiB, filtering 18 GiB, meshing 45 GiB.
  • Treat the working-set peak as an upper bound, not demand. The biggest single process in the bounded run was 89.8 GiB; the 649 GiB is texrecon on 96 threads streaming ~300 GiB of TIFs, and working set counts active page cache. Check the anon vs cache panel before sizing off it.

items.title: Where the wall clock goes
items.text:
46% of the run sits under 3 of 96 cores. Inside the opensfm stage:

Window Duration Median cores What 02:32 - 04:06 94 min 91.4 features + matching pass 1, genuinely parallel 04:08 - 07:48 3h40m ~10 reconstruct, rolling-shutter correct, re-match, reconstruct 07:48 - 09:56 130 min 2.1 undistort

Matching saturates the node. Reconstruction and bundle adjustment are inherently serial. No resource change fixes that.

items.title: Workspace disk
items.text:
--dsm/--dtm profile is multiplier 12, gibPerImage 0.15, maxGiB 2048. estimateWorkspaceGiB takes max(bytes x multiplier, count x gibPerImage) then clamps, so at ~12k the count floor gives ~1800 GiB against ~1400 GiB from bytes. The floor sets the size, the clamp doesn't bind. Confirmed: a 12k run got a 1902 GiB PVC.

Observation % of PVC Absolute Per image opensfm plateau (JPEGs + features) 8.2% 151 GiB Peak, pc-quality low + boundary 29.4% 559 GiB 0.047 GiB Peak, pc-quality medium, unbounded 63.6% ~1200 GiB 0.100 GiB

gibPerImage 0.15 is ~1.5x a measured pc-quality medium run. Size is fine.

Throughput is fine too. Undistort wrote 303 GiB over ~104 min = 40 MiB/s sustained, against the gp3 baseline of 125 MiB/s. Nowhere near capped.

Note

kubelet_volume_stats_used_bytes as a percentage resolves to 0.1%, which is 1.9 GiB on a 1902 GiB volume. Every delta is a multiple of that, so apparent write bursts are quantisation. Use the node-exporter throughput panel for rates.

IOPS might not be, and CPU can't tell you: container CPU excludes iowait, so a job blocked on disk and a job running two threads look identical. 40 MiB/s at the 3000 IOPS baseline is ~14 KiB/op. Check node_disk_io_time_seconds_total (utilisation, 1.0 = saturated) and node_disk_{reads,writes}_completed_total (flat at 3000 = capped). Only raise the class if one of those pins.

If it does: workspaceStorageClass.parameters is passed straight through and Helm deep-merges, so throughput: "500" / iops: "6000" is a values-only change. But StorageClass parameters are immutable, so the class has to be deleted and recreated. Safe between jobs, since it's only read at PVC provisioning time.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Swap only engages when the cgroup hits memory.max. At 720 GiB against a 649 GiB peak it never does and node RAM absorbs it. To make swap absorb a transient, memory.max has to sit below the peak.
  • CPU over-provisioning is free. 76 cores requested against a median of 6.12, but 600 GiB of RAM already selects a 96-vCPU instance so CPU never picks the node, and matching does use all 96. Lowering the request buys nothing.
  • Depth-map estimation runs behind two worker threads, so cores past ~48 only help matching and undistort.
  • With a CPU limit set, ODM gets a matching --max-concurrency, since its default is every node core and would oversubscribe the quota. With no limit (prod) it keeps that default, and an explicit caller value always wins.
  • Workspace PVCs are collected when workflows finish (volumeClaimGC).
  • With plenty of real RAM, skip swap tuning entirely.

items.title: Testing alternative ODM images
items.text:
Workflows normally run config.odmImage. To trial a fork or a new release without redeploying, allowlist the image and pass odmImage per task.

config:
  odmImage: "docker.io/opendronemap/odm:3.6.2"
  allowedOdmImages: "ghcr.io/hotosm/odm,docker.io/opendronemap/odm,docker.io/webodm/odx"

Entries match a repository, not a tag, so any tag or digest of a listed repo is accepted and a new release needs no config change. Bare names are read as Docker Hub, so webodm/odx and docker.io/webodm/odx are the same entry. Matching is exact per repo: webodm/odx-evil and evil.io/webodm/odx are both rejected. An odmImage outside the allowlist is rejected with a 400, and an empty allowedOdmImages rejects every override.

items.title: Submitting a task
items.text:
curl -X POST http://scaleodm:31100/task/new \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "odx-trial",
    "readS3Path": "s3://dronetm-prod/trials/dataset-a/images/",
    "writeS3Path": "s3://dronetm-prod/trials/dataset-a/odx/",
    "odmImage": "webodm/odx",
    "capacityType": "on-demand",
    "options": "[{\"name\":\"sfm-algorithm\",\"value\":\"triangulation\"},{\"name\":\"rolling-shutter\",\"value\":true}]"
  }'

options is a JSON array encoded as a string, matching NodeODM. Each entry becomes --name=value, so only real ODM flags belong there; odmImage and capacityType are top level because they configure the pod, not ODM.

Use on-demand so a spot eviction cannot be mistaken for a crash. The workflow still stops at activeDeadlineSeconds (48h default), so pick a dataset that reaches the dense stage well inside that.

Poll it, then read the logs:

curl http://scaleodm:31100/task/<uuid>/info
kubectl logs -l workflows.argoproj.io/workflow=<uuid> --tail=200

items.title: Flags worth setting
items.text:
Flag Why sfm-algorithm=triangulation Places cameras from GPS instead of adding them one at a time. Needs OpenSfM 1.0, so ODX only. boundary=<AOI GeoJSON> Clips output to one Polygon AOI and can greatly reduce render cost. Pass inline GeoJSON or an s3:// URL; see Boundary. rolling-shutter Corrects the skew from the sensor reading out row by row while the aircraft moves. An electronic shutter at 12 m/s and a 4 cm GSD is ~6 px of skew. ODM holds a readout time per camera model (opendm/rollingshutter.py), but an unlisted camera silently gets a 30 ms guess, so check the log line and set rolling-shutter-readout if the camera is missing. split=400 + split-overlap=150 Caps submodel size on stock ODM, where reconstruction cost grows superlinearly.

sfm-algorithm=triangulation on an image without OpenSfM 1.0 fails at the sparse stage, so change one variable at a time and keep a stock-image run of the same dataset to compare against.

items.title: Flags to avoid on large datasets
items.text:
These buy speed by removing global consistency. Stacked on a 12k-image scene they produced a reconstruction spanning 20 x 13 km over a 3 x 3 km site; dropping them brought it back to 3 x 3 km.

Flag Why not matcher-neighbors=<n> Any value > 0 forces matching_graph_rounds: 0 in ODM/ODX, removing the long-range candidate pairs that make a large block globally rigid. Leave it unset to get 20 rounds (ODX) / 50 (ODM). use-hybrid-bundle-adjustment Sets local_bundle_radius: 1 (immediate neighbours only). Unset gives 0, which uses the global solver. auto-boundary Buffers the convex hull of the camera shots by avg_gsd * 100, where the GSD is in cm but the buffer is applied in metres - a 4.3 cm GSD becomes a 433 m buffer. It rarely trims anything useful.

Independently of any flag, ODX/OpenSfM swaps global bundle adjustment for a stochastic 500-camera-per-round solver above 4,000 shots, and that path holds camera intrinsics fixed - optimize_camera_parameters goes silently inert and cameras.json comes back with every distortion coefficient at 0.0. --split under 4,000 images is the only way to get focal length and distortion refined.

items.title: Defects no flag can fix
items.text:
Measured on a 12,000-image project flown with four DJI Mini 4 Pro airframes. All three need fixing at ingest, before ODM sees the imagery.

  • The altitude datum resets on every power cycle. AbsoluteAltitude is RelativeAltitude plus a constant fixed at power-on: across 36 flights the difference had a standard deviation of 0.0000 in 33 of them. Two flights over the same ground 37 minutes apart reported altitudes 92 m apart, median 41 m across all co-located pairs. ODM picks matching candidates in 3D, so repeat passes over the same ground drop out of each other's candidate list and never match. Use RelativeAltitude, or normalise onto one datum against a DEM and write it back into the EXIF, since ODM reads the file and not your database.
  • Digital zoom does not change the reported focal length. DigitalZoomRatio was 2 on 11.9% of images, which on a Mini 4 Pro is a sensor crop, yet FocalLength, FocalLengthIn35mmFormat and FOV were identical on every image. ODM fits one camera model across images whose real focal length differs by 2x. Drop the zoomed frames, or rewrite their EXIF focal so ODM builds a second camera model - dropping 12% of a set punches holes if the zoom is interleaved rather than whole flights.
  • Nadir is not -90. Gimbal pitch was exactly -80.0 on 12,145 of 12,338 images, consistent across all four aircraft, so it is the platform and not a crew choice. A filter expressed as a tolerance around -90 will not do what it says. Derive the held angle from the data.

A 249 g airframe with an electronic shutter, no RTK and SurveyingMode: 0 will not match survey-grade kit whatever flags it is processed with.

items.title: Notes
items.text: Tasks submitted this way are invisible to Drone TM: its reconcile looks up odm_task_uuid in its own database, so read results from the workflow logs and the writeS3Path prefix. POST /task/restart reuses the task's odmImage, re-checked against allowedOdmImages, so a restart fails with a 400 if the image has since been removed from the allowlist.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Everything runs against the real stack (DB, S3, Kubernetes) via Docker Compose. No mocks.

# start services, then run the whole suite
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.test.yaml up -d db s3
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.test.yaml run --rm api

# one package
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.test.yaml run --rm api go test -v ./app/meta/...

# E2E, behind a build tag
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.test.yaml run --rm api go test -v -tags=e2e .

items.title: Layout
items.text:
• Integration (app/*/*_test.go) against a real database, S3 and Kubernetes.
  • E2E (main_test.go) full system scenarios.

Helpers per package:

  • testDB(t) database connection with cleanup (app/api, app/meta, app/db)
  • testWorkflowClient(t) real Argo Workflows client (app/api)
  • testutil.TestDBURL() reads SCALEODM_DATABASE_URL
func TestFeature(t *testing.T) {
    db, cleanup := testDB(t)
    defer cleanup()

    store := meta.NewStore(db)
    // ...
}

items.title: Test data
items.text:
• Database: SCALEODM_DATABASE_URL, same var as prod. Tests clean up after themselves.
  • S3: AWS_S3_ENDPOINT, the RustFS instance in the compose stack.
  • Kubernetes: needs a real cluster (Talos) with Argo Workflows installed.

items.title: When something breaks
items.text:
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.test.yaml ps           # services up?
psql postgres://odm:odm@localhost:31101/scaleodm?sslmode=disable # DB reachable?
kubectl get pods -n argo                                         # Argo alive?

items.title: Markdown Architectural Decision Records
items.text: Markdown Architectural Decision Records documenting the technical decisions taken in this project.

items.title: Decisions
items.text:
• 0000 - HOTOSM Context and Alignment
  • 0001 - Argo Workflows
  • 0002 - AWS S3
  • 0003 - Swap-based Memory Sizing
  • 0004 - Plain Logs Instead of Built-in OpenTelemetry

items.title: Higher Level HOTOSM Decisions
items.text:
Many decisions have been made at an organizational level, affecting all tools that we develop.

The decisions made in this project should not deviate much from the choices, starting here.

items.title: Use Kubernetes-Native Argo Workflows Instead of NodeODM + ClusterODM
path: Use Kubernetes-Native Argo Workflows Instead of NodeODM + ClusterODM

items.title: Context and Problem Statement
items.text:
ScaleODM's goal is to provide a cloud-native, auto-scaling orchestration layer for OpenDroneMap (ODM). The existing OpenDroneMap ecosystem provides two key tools:

  • NodeODM: Runs individual ODM jobs as a REST API service.
  • ClusterODM: Distributes jobs across multiple NodeODM instances.

While both are robust and widely adopted, they were not designed for Kubernetes-native environments. Running NodeODM and ClusterODM inside Kubernetes introduced several challenges:

  • ClusterODM scales VMs, not containers, and doesn't leverage Kubernetes Jobs, Deployments, or Autoscalers.
  • NodeODM's queueing system is file-based and not distributed.
  • Data ingestion depends on uploading imagery via HTTP or providing a zip_url, adding I/O overhead and making it harder to integrate with S3.
  • The NodeODM container model (long-running servers with stateful projects) doesn't fit Kubernetes' ephemeral job model.

We need a system that can:

  • Orchestrate ODM workloads as ephemeral, stateless jobs.
  • Scale horizontally using native Kubernetes primitives.
  • Integrate cleanly with S3 for both input and output data.
  • Maintain API compatibility with NodeODM for client interoperability.
path: Use Kubernetes-Native Argo Workflows Instead of NodeODM + ClusterODM

items.title: Considered Options
items.text:
• Continue using ClusterODM + NodeODM inside Kubernetes.
  • Wrap NodeODM with a custom queue and scaling layer (e.g. PostgreSQL-based).
  • Replace NodeODM/ClusterODM orchestration with Kubernetes-native Argo Workflows.
path: Use Kubernetes-Native Argo Workflows Instead of NodeODM + ClusterODM

items.title: Decision Outcome
items.text:
We chose to replace NodeODM + ClusterODM orchestration with Kubernetes-native Argo Workflows.

Each ODM processing task is defined as a workflow that runs:

  1. A download step to sync imagery from S3.
  2. A processing step using the standard ODM container.
  3. An upload step to push final artifacts back to S3.

This workflow model maps naturally to Kubernetes' scheduling, scaling, and failure recovery mechanisms. It also simplifies the system by removing the need for custom queueing, stateful NodeODM instances, or VM-level scaling.

Argo Workflows natively supports:

  • Long-running, resumable, and observable pipelines.
  • Native retry, TTL cleanup, and artifact management.
  • Declarative YAML specifications compatible with CI/CD tooling.
  • Native integration with Kubernetes Secrets, Volumes, and ServiceAccounts.
path: Use Kubernetes-Native Argo Workflows Instead of NodeODM + ClusterODM

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• ✅ processing jobs are now stateless, isolated, and restartable.
  • ✅ scaling is handled entirely by Kubernetes (HPA, KEDA, etc.).
  • ✅ S3 becomes the single source of truth for inputs and outputs.
  • ✅ NodeODM-compatible API means existing tooling like pyODM should work.
  • ✅ federation (multi-cluster job delegation) becomes straightforward.
  • ❌ Argo Workflows introduces additional CRD complexity and controller overhead.
  • ❌ ScaleODM becomes entirely dependent on Kubernetes and installing Argo workflows into the cluster environment.
path: Use Kubernetes-Native Argo Workflows Instead of NodeODM + ClusterODM

items.title: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows
path: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows

items.title: Context and Problem Statement
items.text: Each ODM (OpenDroneMap) job in ScaleODM needs to download raw imagery from S3 and upload processed outputs back to S3. The system uses Argo Workflows for long-running processing jobs, often lasting hours or days.
path: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows

items.title: Considered Options
items.text:
• Use long-lived static AWS credentials in Kubernetes Secrets.
  • Use short-lived AWS STS credentials per workflow.
  • Use pre-signed URLs for each job's S3 read/write operations.
path: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows

items.title: Decision Outcome
items.text:
We chose to use static S3 credentials stored in a Kubernetes Secret, referenced by workflow pods via secretKeyRef. This was chosen over STS temporary credentials because:

  • ODM jobs can run for many hours and may be queued for extended periods before starting. STS session tokens (max 12h) can expire before a queued job begins processing, causing silent failures.
  • The attack surface is small: credentials are only accessible within the Kubernetes cluster via the Secret API, never inlined in Argo Workflow specs.
  • Operational simplicity: no IAM role trust policies, no STS endpoint configuration, no per-job credential generation.
path: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows

items.title: How it works
items.text:
1. The operator creates a Kubernetes Secret (scaleodm-secrets) in the ScaleODM release namespace containing AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and AWS_DEFAULT_REGION. In the unified runtime secret contract this same secret also contains SCALEODM_DATABASE_URL and AWS_S3_ENDPOINT.
  2. ScaleODM builds Argo Workflow specs that reference this secret via secretKeyRef env vars - credentials are resolved at pod startup, not baked into the workflow manifest.
  3. All workflow containers (download, process, upload, cleanup) use rclone with env_auth = true to pick up credentials from the environment.
path: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows

items.title: Example Argo workflow env vars
items.text:
env:
  - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: scaleodm-secrets
        key: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
  - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: scaleodm-secrets
        key: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
  - name: AWS_DEFAULT_REGION
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: scaleodm-secrets
        key: AWS_DEFAULT_REGION
        optional: true
path: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Credentials are never visible in kubectl get workflow -o yaml.
  • No expiry concerns for long-running or queued jobs.
  • Single credential pair for both read and write operations (same IAM user/role needs s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on the relevant buckets).
  • Credential rotation requires updating the Kubernetes Secret and restarting affected pods.
path: S3 Credential Management for Argo Workflows

items.title: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: Context and Problem Statement
items.text:
ScaleODM sizes each ODM process pod from the image count, using a fitted table in app/workflows/standard.go. That table predicts the peak working set: a brief spike (notably mvs-texturing) that lasts seconds to minutes, not the steady-state resident set.

Previously the pod requested the whole peak as real RAM (request ~= limit, Guaranteed QoS). This over-provisioned nodes badly. Field data:

  • 3000 images peaked at ~144Gi but ran fine on a 62Gi RAM + 127Gi swap host.
  • 5000 images ran on ~62Gi RAM + swap, versus a ~227Gi estimated peak.

Provisioning the full peak as RAM means paying for 3-4x the RAM actually resident for all but a few seconds of the job.
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: Considered Options
items.text:
• Request the full peak as RAM (status quo). Simple and safe, but wastes large amounts of RAM and caps how many images a given machine can process.
  • Request steady-state RAM, absorb the peak with swap. Request a fraction of the peak and let the kernel spill the brief spike to disk swap under Kubernetes' LimitedSwap policy.
  • Lower the estimates outright. Rejected: the peak is real and would OOM-kill without swap to catch it.
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: Decision Outcome
items.text:
We request the steady-state RAM and let swap catch the brief peak:

request (real RAM) = peak / (1 + SWAP_RATIO)             # prod ratio 1.0, so ~1/2 of peak
limit (swap on)    = request * (1 + MARGIN_PERCENT/100)  # a resident cap below node RAM
limit (swap off)   = peak * (1 + MARGIN_PERCENT/100)     # whole peak as RAM

The limit is the container's memory.max, which caps resident (non-swapped) memory. With swap on it must sit below node RAM (Karpenter sizes the node off the request), so the kernel is forced to push the peak's overflow into swap and the node never fills up. Because request < limit the pod is Burstable QoS and gets a swap grant - Guaranteed pods (request == limit) get none. Nodes provide swap (AWS via the Karpenter EC2NodeClass, other clusters via a disk swapfile).

This lets 5000 images request ~114Gi RAM (peak 227 / 2) + swap instead of a ~227Gi RAM node.
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Swap is split into two independent layers so the same build runs anywhere:

  • Node layer: swap exists on the node and kubelet allows it (failSwapOn: false, NodeSwap feature gate, swapBehavior: LimitedSwap). The node also sets vm.swappiness=10: swap is only needed for the brief peak, so low swappiness keeps ODM's hot working set in RAM during the long steady-state stages and only spills at the peak. Note swappiness biases reclaim toward or away from anon pages even under memory.max pressure, so 10 is a benchmark vs the 60 default. Provisioned per-platform.
  • Workload layer: the pod declares request < limit. Platform-agnostic; ScaleODM never needs to know how a node got its swap.

Each workflow is annotated with scaleodm.hotosm.org/burst-headroom-gib (limit - request) as a rough guide. The real per-pod swap allowance is container_swap_limit_bytes (LimitedSwap grants it proportionally).

Setup and tuning knobs are in docs/swap.md.
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: Why it stays safe
items.text:
The container limit is a resident cap that targets below node RAM. When resident hits it, memcg reclaim pushes the overflow to swap, so the node doesn't fill up. This matters because kubelet's node-pressure eviction is swap-blind - its memory.available ignores swap, so free swap alone can't stop it. The old peak-based limit (~2x node RAM) gave the pod no memcg reclaim boundary at all; resident climbed into node RAM and eviction fired even with swap free. (Why node-level global reclaim didn't save it is unproven - the failed run lacked telemetry.)

Backing it up:

  • Swap = 2x node RAM on fast NVMe - plenty to hold the overflow, quick to page.
  • LimitedSwap grants swap proportionally: pod swap = (request / node RAM) * node swap. So node RAM must stay close to the request, or the pod gets too little swap. Selection is driven by RAM (not CPU) to keep that ratio high.
  • Node reclaim tuning (vm.min_free_kbytes, vm.watermark_scale_factor) makes kswapd start early, so a fast fusion spike can't outrun reclaim into eviction.

Containment vs completion. Containment: when the limit lands below node RAM, a node-level eviction (and NotReady risk) becomes a contained, single-pod event. This is not guaranteed at every node size - ScaleODM doesn't know which node Karpenter picks, so a request just under a node's allocatable leaves no room for the margin and the limit can land above node RAM (e.g. request 113Gi on a 128Gi node -> limit 136Gi). Node reclaim tuning is the backstop there; watch such jobs. Completion: not guaranteed either - if too much of fusion's working set is active (not swappable), the limit turns the eviction into a contained cgroup OOM. Field data suggests it's mostly swappable (the ~144Gi peak on a 62Gi RAM + swap host above), but validate before relying on it: verify memory.swap.max is roughly the expected proportional grant (not just > 0), then watch one real large job - swap climbs, memory.events shows no OOM, node stays above 100Mi - before trusting it. If it OOMs, levers in order: lower SWAP_RATIO (bigger request = more RAM + bigger swap share), then more node swap.
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Nodes are provisioned for the resident set, not the peak, cutting RAM cost and raising the images-per-machine ceiling substantially.
  • The estimate extrapolates beyond the 5000-image table (last-segment slope, ~0.043 GiB/image) instead of clamping, so large jobs are sized realistically. MEMORY_MAX_GIB bounds it to what the pool can schedule. At ratio 1.0 (request = peak/2) the ceiling for a 256Gi r-family NVMe node (e.g. r6id.8xlarge
  • 2x swap) is ~8-9k images (peak ~380Gi, ~190Gi RAM request). Beyond that needs bigger-RAM instances, out of scope for this pool.
  • Nodes must provide swap. Without it, a Burstable pod that exceeds its request is OOM-killed at the peak. Enforced on AWS by the swap-enabled EC2NodeClass; on other clusters it is an operator responsibility (docs/swap.md).
  • On AWS, ScaleODM runs on a dedicated tainted pool (pool=scaleodm) so the NVMe/swap nodes are isolated from other workloads and one big job can't starve the shared pool's capacity. See docs/swap.md.
  • Peak-time performance degrades while swapping (disk is slower than RAM), but on AWS the swap is on local NVMe instance store (*id families), ~100x faster than EBS, so heavy paging stays acceptable.
  • Effective OOM headroom depends on the proportional swap formula above, so SWAP_RATIO should be validated per real workload rather than trusted blindly.
  • SWAP_RATIO=0 restores the old behaviour (request the full peak as RAM) for clusters without swap.
  • A job that gets OOM-killed mid-run but reports success is not necessarily fine: OpenMVS surviving an OOM may mean a subprocess or optional stage was skipped. Validation must check expected outputs (orthophoto, DSM, point cloud) and kernel OOM counters (dmesg / node_vmstat_oom_kill), not just the workflow's final status.
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: CPU sizing
items.text:
Node selection is driven by RAM. CPU is requested per GiB of the RAM request at the r-family ratio (CPU_PER_GIB=0.125, 1 vCPU per 8Gi), so the CPU request always fits the RAM-selected r-node and never forces a bigger instance.

In production the CPU limit is omitted (CPU_LIMIT_MULTIPLIER=0), so ODM bursts to every core on the node (ODM defaults its concurrency to all detected CPUs, and we pass no --max-concurrency flag). Where a limit is set, ScaleODM passes a --max-concurrency matching it so ODM does not oversubscribe the quota. The generic chart default keeps CPU_LIMIT_MULTIPLIER=1.5 (a bounded limit) as the safe out-of-the-box value; set it to 0 to allow bursting. CPU therefore affects only speed, never feasibility, and a --split submodel workflow is not needed for scheduling (it remains a possible future wall-clock optimisation).
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: Spot vs on-demand
items.text: Jobs at or above ONDEMAND_IMAGE_THRESHOLD (5000) are auto-upgraded from spot to on-demand, because they run for hours and a spot eviction would waste the whole run. Smaller jobs stay on cheap spot. An explicit on-demand request is always honoured.
path: Swap-based Memory Sizing for ODM Jobs

items.title: Plain Logs Instead of Built-in OpenTelemetry
path: Plain Logs Instead of Built-in OpenTelemetry

items.title: Context and Problem Statement
items.text:
ScaleODM used to ship an optional OpenTelemetry module (app/observability). It pushed OTLP traces and metrics for the API: request counts and latency, submission failures, reconciliation and readiness counters.

On review, we determined it didn't add much benefit:

  • The Argo controller, cAdvisor and kube-state-metrics already tell us job counts, phases, durations, failures, OOM kills and resource use. That's what our Grafana dashboard is built on.
  • The traces only covered the API, not the ODM processing itself (the part that actually goes wrong), and were sampled at 10%.
  • Metrics are just counts. When a job fails, what we want to know is which request it was and what was in it, so we can replay it. The logs already have that.
  • To use it at all, we'd have needed an OTLP collector in the cluster, as the gRPC exporters don't fit the usual Prometheus scrape setup.
path: Plain Logs Instead of Built-in OpenTelemetry

items.title: Considered Options
items.text:
• Keep the OTel module. It's vendor-neutral, but it's ~450 lines plus a pile of dependencies to maintain, for signals we mostly already have.
  • Swap it for a Prometheus /metrics endpoint. This fits how everything else in the cluster is scraped, but we'd still be keeping metrics nobody looks at.
  • Remove it and rely on logs. ScaleODM only runs on Kubernetes, so anyone deploying it already has (or should have) something collecting container logs, like Loki.
path: Plain Logs Instead of Built-in OpenTelemetry

items.title: Decision Outcome
items.text:
We removed the module.

ScaleODM just logs to stdout, including the request parameters and a stable reason=<code> when a /task/new call is rejected. Collecting, searching and alerting on those logs is left to whatever log stack the cluster runs.
path: Plain Logs Instead of Built-in OpenTelemetry

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• No app-level metrics or traces. Cluster metrics (Argo, cAdvisor, kube-state-metrics) are still where dashboards come from.
  • Failures are found and replayed from the logs, e.g. in Loki: {namespace="odm"} |= "rejected reason=".
  • Alerting on failure rates comes from log rules (e.g. the Loki ruler), rather than app counters.
  • If we ever do need per-request metrics, the simplest option is a Prometheus /metrics endpoint with a ServiceMonitor, not an OTLP push pipeline.
path: Plain Logs Instead of Built-in OpenTelemetry
